measurements.name: on-CPU time vs /proc/<tid>/schedstat (kernel cfs accounting)
measurements.threshold_basis: 0.5% median; the same kernel field, read independently

measurements.name: preempted time vs /proc/<tid>/schedstat (kernel run-queue delay)
measurements.threshold_basis: 100 us absolute median; the value itself is ~40 us, so a relative threshold is meaningless

measurements.name: on-CPU time vs /proc/<tid>/stat utime+stime (tick granularity)
measurements.threshold_basis: 4 clock ticks (10 ms each) over the window

measurements.name: wall time vs CLOCK_MONOTONIC read by the verifier
measurements.threshold_basis: 1% median; the two reads are a few microseconds apart

measurements.name: blocked time vs wall minus on-CPU (sleeping window)
measurements.threshold_basis: 1% median; a sleeping thread is on-CPU for ~0

measurements.name: the trace's preempted total vs the tier's own cumulative
measurements.threshold_basis: 5% median; the trace holds the differences of the tier's counter, so the two must agree. The trace's starts at each thread's first sample and the tier's at the program load, so the trace's is the smaller one

measurements.name: preempted time vs perf sched timehist 'sch delay' column (reported, not gated)
measurements.threshold_basis: 10% median; perf-sched(1) defines 'sch delay' as the time between wakeup and actually running. The kernel's run_delay and perf's sch delay are both run-queue waits but are not identical: the kernel accumulates continuously, perf only where it captured a sched_wakeup tracepoint. So perf's sch delay is a LOWER BOUND on PACE's preempted, and the gap between them grows with the contention: a thread that was already runnable and got switched out accrues kernel run_delay but no perf sch delay. The gap is therefore a property of how oversubscribed the machine is, not of the library, and a fixed threshold cannot be right for every machine. The check is therefore one-sided: it fails only if perf's sch delay EXCEEDS PACE's preempted, which would mean PACE under-reports the run-queue wait. The other direction is the known definitional gap. The check below is the tight one, because it compares the same quantity on both sides.

measurements.name: off-CPU time (preempted + blocked) vs perf 'wait time' column
measurements.threshold_basis: 5% median; perf-sched(1) defines 'wait time' as the time between sched-out and next sched-in, which is exactly PACE's preempted + blocked. The check is one-sided because PACE's window is inside perf's recording: the trace's first sample establishes the baseline, so the head of the recording is not counted, and the last sample's window may be partial. So PACE's total is expected to be the smaller of the two, and the check fails only if PACE's exceeds perf's, which would mean PACE over-reports.

measurements.name: on-CPU time vs perf sched timehist 'run time' column
measurements.threshold_basis: 2% median; perf-sched(1) defines 'run time' as the time the task actually ran, reconstructed from sched_switch tracepoints

measurements.name: decomposition balance on a recorded trace
measurements.threshold_basis: 0.01% median; the sum of buckets against the wall time
